content.content: Db database 22 . c Simulations for various CPY expression levels and misfolding ratios with the constraint for retro-translocation enzymes. Source data are provided as a Source Data file. Here, we used the maximum growth rate reduction to indicate the fitness cost of CPY going through different routes: 1) all correctly folded and targeted to the vacuole without misfolding; 2) misfolded in different ratios and some targeted for ERAD (here we use 45% misfolding ratio to represent the native degradation ratio 33 and 100% misfolding ratio for fully misfolded form CPY*); 3) all misfolded and retained in the ER for different times. Our simulations showed that misfolding imposes more fitness cost compared with correct folding; that retention imposes more fitness cost compared with ERAD; and that retention in the ER for a longer time would also impose more fitness cost (Fig. 3b ). The model predicted that a lower level of misfolded CPY (native level CPY expression, 100% misfolded) has a smaller impact on cell growth. However, when misfolded CPY is expressed in larger amounts (25-fold CPY expression, 100% misfolded), there is a higher fitness cost. The simulation is consistent with experimental observations 32 . If the misfolded proteins are degraded by ERAD and the proteasome, then amino acids and modification precursors such as glycans can be recycled. However, if misfolded proteins are retained in the ER, they would compete with unfolded proteins for limited ER quality control machineries especially Kar2 and Pdi1 32 , which would lower the processing rate of correctly folded proteins and increase the ER burden. We investigated the simulated various protein levels and found that the levels of Kar2 and Pdi1 increase significantly when CPY is retained (Supplementary Fig. 3 ), which suggests that the retained protein would drain Kar2 and Pdi1 and therefore compete with native proteins processed in the secretory pathway. In addition, we evaluated the ER redox stress by comparing the transport of glutathione (GSH) and glutathione disulfide (GSSG) and found that the flux of GSSG export from the ER is significantly higher when misfolded protein is retained in the ER (Supplementary Fig. 4 ), suggesting the higher redox unbalance in the ER at this state. The simulated transport increase is also in line with experimental observations 34 . Furthermore, we performed analyses to identify parameters leading to misfolded protein accumulation in the ER (Supplementary Fig. 5a–d , Fig. 3c ). When retro-translocation enzymes (Doa10 and Hrd1 complexes) were constrained, the excessive misfolded CPY would be retained and accumulated in the ER when CPY was expressed at high levels, causing a steeper decrease in the specific growth rate (Fig. 3c ). Other parameters such as ERAD capacity, ER volume, ER membrane space, and secretory machinery capacity were not able to show the retention and accumulation phenotype when constrained in the model (Supplementary Fig. 5a–d ). We found that the retention of the misfolded protein phenotype is alleviated when removing the constraint of retro-translocation enzymes, suggesting the importance of retro-translocation toward handling of misfolded proteins (Supplementary Fig. 5e ). Therefore, we can use pcSecYeast with the extra constraint on retro-translocation enzymes to mimic various states of misfolded protein accumulation in the ER (Fig. 3c ). The plateau in the CPY degradation rate demonstrates that there is a maximum capacity of the retro-translocation and therefore also a tolerance limit for misfolded CPY. Protein features impact recombinant protein production Different secretory proteins are processed by different components of the secretory pathway based on their amino acid composition and PTMs. To identify the factors that influence secreted protein levels, we expanded pcSecYeast to describe the production of eight different recombinant proteins by adding the corresponding recombinant protein production and secretion reactions, respectively. These eight recombinant proteins differ in protein size and PTMs (Fig. 4a , detailed information in Supplementary Data 7 ). Note that hemoglobin folds with heme as a prosthetic group, which requires balancing of heme biosynthesis and its recombinant protein production (Fig. 4a ) 35 . We generated eight specific models to simulate the maximum recombinant protein secretion under various growth rates. We observed that the maximum production rates were achieved at low specific growth rates for all the studied recombinant proteins (Fig. 4b ), consistent with previous reports of bell shape kinetics for recombinant protein production in S. cerevisiae and Pichia pastoris 36 – 40 . Insulin precursor (IP) and α-amylase production were reported as growth-dependent 41 , but only for the investigation of a more narrow interval of specific growth rates (0.05-0.2 h −1 ), which is consistent with the model simulations. At high specific growth rates, there is a clear drop of production rate for all recombinant proteins (Fig. 4b ), which clearly shows that at high specific growth rates the cell prioritizes its limited capacity of the secretory pathway to native proteins. It is important to note that a basic GEM can only describe a linear negative correlation of recombinant protein production with increasing specific growth rates (Supplementary Fig. 6 ). Moreover, the fact that the simulated α-amylase production by the basic GEM is around 30 times higher than experimental values 42 , even with the measured glucose uptake rate as a constraint, highlights that basic GEMs are unfit for recombinant protein simulation (Supplementary Fig. 6 ). Source data are provided as a Source Data file. We additionally investigated which protein feature influences recombinant protein production the most through a parameter importance analysis by machine learning. We found that PTMs on average have a higher impact on recombinant protein production compared with amino acid composition (Fig. 4c , Supplementary Fig. 7 for fivefold cross validation). Among all simulated features, O -glycosylation and N -glycosylation have larger negative impacts on recombinant protein production, which suggests that having more glycosylation sites would cause more burden for the cell (Fig. 4c ). FSEOF identifies overexpression targets for recombinant protein overproduction Identifying engineering targets is crucial to improve the specific recombinant protein production rate. Predicting gene overexpression targets is more difficult and complex than predicting gene deletion targets since amplification of gene expression does not always increase the metabolic fluxes 43 . To fully validate the predictive power of pcSecYeast, we used the generated recombinant protein-specific models to predict overexpression targets for increasing recombinant protein production. Target prediction was performed using adapted Flux Scanning based on Enforced Objective Function (FSEOF) 43 , where the model was constrained with a stepwise decrease in the specific growth rate, and recombinant protein production was maximized. The original FSEOF method selects fluxes that increase with the enforcement of recombinant protein production in the GEM simulations and identifies those reactions and associated genes as overexpression targets. Since we can compute the protein levels from the pcSecYeast simulations, we can directly select proteins, as overexpression targets, whose increased levels would result in increased recombinant protein production (Fig. 5a and Supplementary Data 8 – 15 for prediction results of these eight recombinant proteins). The predicted overexpression targets were ranked with priority scores and compared among the eight recombinant proteins (Fig. 5b, c ). We predicted average 117 overexpression targets for each of the eight recombinant proteins with the majority of them (80%) being in the secretory pathway and 20% in the metabolic part of the model (Fig. 5b, c ). The identified targets were more likely shared by recombinant proteins when they have the same PTMs. For example, targets in the O -glycosylation pathway were shared by O -glycosylated human-transferrin (HTF) and human granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (hGCSF) (Fig. 5c ). Surprisingly, even though insulin precursor (IP) contains no N -glycosylation site, some predicted overexpression targets are related to N -glycosylation. This is explained by the fact that N -glycosylation is required for some secretory machinery proteins such as Pdi1 which catalyzes disulfide bond formation in IP production. By removing the disulfide bonds in IP, we found that those N-glycosylation-related genes were no longer predicted as targets (Supplementary Data 16 ). There are 41 predicted targets shared by all eight proteins, which are mainly involved in sorting, ER-Golgi transport and translocation from cytosol to the ER, suggesting the general importance of these processes in protein secretion (Fig. 5c ). We also showed that hemoglobin is the recombinant protein with multiple unique targets in metabolism, especially for heme production, which demonstrates that metabolism is equally important along with the secretory pathway for improving hemoglobin production. For all other recombinant proteins, the secretory pathway is more limiting according to the prediction. content.content:
TITLE: Genome-scale reconstructions of the mammalian secretory pathway predict metabolic costs and limitations of protein secretion. J: Nature communications 2020 DOI: 10.1038/s41467-019-13867-y PMCID: PMC6940358 ABS: In mammalian cells, >25% of synthesized proteins are exported through the secretory pathway. The pathway complexity, however, obfuscates its impact on the secretion of different proteins. Unraveling its impact on diverse proteins is particularly important for biopharmaceutical production. Here we delineate the core secretory pathway functions and integrate them with genome-scale metabolic reconstructions of human, mouse, and Chinese hamster ovary cells. The resulting reconstructions enable the computation of energetic costs and machinery demands of each secreted protein. By integrating additional omics data, we find that highly secretory cells have adapted to reduce expression and secretion of other expensive host cell proteins. Furthermore, we predict metabolic costs and maximum productivities of biotherapeutic proteins and identify protein features that most significantly impact protein secretion. Finally, the model successfully predicts the increase in secretion of a monoclonal antibody after silencing a highly expressed selection marker. This work represents a knowledgebase of the mammalian secretory pathway that serves as a novel tool for systems biotechnology. TITLE: Genome-scale modeling of the protein secretory machinery in yeast. J: PloS one 2013 DOI: 10.1371/journal.pone.0063284 PMCID: PMC3646752 ABS: The protein secretory machinery in Eukarya is involved in post-translational modification (PTMs) and sorting of the secretory and many transmembrane proteins. While the secretory machinery has been well-studied using classic reductionist approaches, a holistic view of its complex nature is lacking. Here, we present the first genome-scale model for the yeast secretory machinery which captures the knowledge generated through more than 50 years of research. The model is based on the concept of a Protein Specific Information Matrix (PSIM: characterized by seven PTMs features). An algorithm was developed which mimics secretory machinery and assigns each secretory protein to a particular secretory class that determines the set of PTMs and transport steps specific to each protein. Protein abundances were integrated with the model in order to gain system level estimation of the metabolic demands associated with the processing of each specific protein as well as a quantitative estimation of the activity of each component of the secretory machinery. TITLE: Genome wide analysis of protein production load in Trichoderma reesei. J: Biotechnology for biofuels 2016 DOI: 10.1186/s13068-016-0547-5 PMCID: PMC4924338 ABS:

Background

The filamentous fungus Trichoderma reesei (teleomorph Hypocrea jecorina) is a widely used industrial host organism for protein production. In industrial cultivations, it can produce over 100 g/l of extracellular protein, mostly constituting of cellulases and hemicellulases. In order to improve protein production of T. reesei the transcriptional regulation of cellulases and secretory pathway factors have been extensively studied. However, the metabolism of T. reesei under protein production conditions has not received much attention.

Results

To understand the physiology and metabolism of T. reesei under protein production conditions we carried out a well-controlled bioreactor experiment with extensive analysis. We used minimal media to make the data amenable for modelling and three strain pairs to cover different protein production levels. With RNA-sequencing transcriptomics we detected the concentration of the carbon source as the most important determinant of the transcriptome. As the major transcriptional response concomitant to protein production we detected the induction of selected genes that were putatively regulated by xyr1 and were related to protein transport, amino acid metabolism and transcriptional regulation. We found novel metabolic responses such as production of glycerol and a cellotriose-like compound. We then used this cultivation data for flux balance analysis of T. reesei metabolism and demonstrate for the first time the use of genome wide stoichiometric metabolic modelling for T. reesei. We show that our model can predict protein production rate and provides novel insight into the metabolism of protein production. We also provide this unprecedented cultivation and transcriptomics data set for future modelling efforts.

Conclusions

The use of stoichiometric modelling can open a novel path for the improvement of protein production in T. reesei. Based on this we propose sulphur assimilation as a major limiting factor of protein production. As an organism with exceptional protein production capabilities modelling of T. reesei can provide novel insight also to other less productive organisms. TITLE: Inferring secretory and metabolic pathway activity from omic data with secCellFie. J: Metabolic engineering 2024 DOI: 10.1016/j.ymben.2023.12.006 PMCID: PMC11177574 ABS: Understanding protein secretion has considerable importance in biotechnology and important implications in a broad range of normal and pathological conditions including development, immunology, and tissue function. While great progress has been made in studying individual proteins in the secretory pathway, measuring and quantifying mechanistic changes in the pathway's activity remains challenging due to the complexity of the biomolecular systems involved. Systems biology has begun to address this issue with the development of algorithmic tools for analyzing biological pathways; however most of these tools remain accessible only to experts in systems biology with extensive computational experience. Here, we expand upon the user-friendly CellFie tool which quantifies metabolic activity from omic data to include secretory pathway functions, allowing any scientist to infer properties of protein secretion from omic data. We demonstrate how the secretory expansion of CellFie (secCellFie) can help predict metabolic and secretory functions across diverse immune cells, hepatokine secretion in a cell model of NAFLD, and antibody production in Chinese Hamster Ovary cells. TITLE: Predicting the expression of recombinant monoclonal antibodies in Chinese hamster ovary cells based on sequence features of the CDR3 domain. J: Biotechnology progress 2014 DOI: 10.1002/btpr.1839 PMCID: None ABS: Despite the development of high-titer bioprocesses capable of producing >10 g L(-1) of recombinant monoclonal antibody (MAb), some so called "difficult-to-express" (DTE) MAbs only reach much lower process titers. For widely utilized "platform" processes the only discrete variable is the protein coding sequence of the recombinant product. However, there has been little systematic study to identify the sequence parameters that affect expression. This information is vital, as it would allow us to rationally design genetic sequence and engineering strategies for optimal bioprocessing. We have therefore developed a new computational tool that enables prediction of MAb titer in Chinese hamster ovary (CHO) cells based on the recombinant coding sequence of the expressed MAb. Model construction utilized a panel of MAbs, which following a 10-day fed-batch transient production process varied in titer 5.6-fold, allowing analysis of the sequence features that impact expression over a range of high and low MAb productivity. The model identified 18 light chain (LC)-specific sequence features within complementarity determining region 3 (CDR3) capable of predicting MAb titer with a root mean square error of 0.585 relative expression units. Furthermore, we identify that CDR3 variation influences the rate of LC-HC dimerization during MAb synthesis, which could be exploited to improve the production of DTE MAb variants via increasing the transfected LC:HC gene ratio. Taken together these data suggest that engineering intervention strategies to improve the expression of DTE recombinant products can be rationally implemented based on an identification of the sequence motifs that render a recombinant product DTE. TITLE: Massively parallel interrogation of protein fragment secretability using SECRiFY reveals features influencing secretory system transit. J: Nature communications 2021 DOI: 10.1038/s41467-021-26720-y PMCID: PMC8571348 ABS: While transcriptome- and proteome-wide technologies to assess processes in protein biogenesis are now widely available, we still lack global approaches to assay post-ribosomal biogenesis events, in particular those occurring in the eukaryotic secretory system. We here develop a method, SECRiFY, to simultaneously assess the secretability of >105 protein fragments by two yeast species, S. cerevisiae and P. pastoris, using custom fragment libraries, surface display and a sequencing-based readout. Screening human proteome fragments with a median size of 50-100 amino acids, we generate datasets that enable datamining into protein features underlying secretability, revealing a striking role for intrinsic disorder and chain flexibility. The SECRiFY methodology generates sufficient amounts of annotated data for advanced machine learning methods to deduce secretability patterns. The finding that secretability is indeed a learnable feature of protein sequences provides a solid base for application-focused studies. TITLE: Toward Rational Design of Precision-Fermented Milk Proteins: Integrating Cross-Species Selection, Post-Translational Modification, and AI Optimization. J: Comprehensive reviews in food science and food safety 2026 DOI: 10.1111/1541-4337.70618 PMCID: PMC13500877 ABS: Milk proteins deliver nutritional, functional, and bioactive properties that alternative protein sources cannot adequately replicate, yet conventional livestock-based production faces compounding constraints of scalability, resource intensity, and sustainability. Precision fermentation offers a structurally distinct solution, but existing reviews have addressed neither a systematic cross-species framework for target selection nor a treatment of post-translational modifications (PTMs) gap-bridging, leaving critical gaps in rational pipeline design. This review integrates four analyses: a cross-species comparison of sequence, structural, and PTMs characteristics across human, bovine, goat, and camel milk proteins to inform target prioritization; a consolidation of advances in host engineering, fermentation scale-up, and downstream purification; a structural-functional comparison of precision-fermented and native milk proteins encompassing phosphorylation, disulfide bond pairing, and glycosylation fidelity, alongside strategies for bridging identified PTMs gaps; and an evaluation of AI-driven optimization strategies for heterologous milk protein expression. Cross-species analysis favors human-derived sequences for infant nutrition and immunity, while ruminant proteins excel in expression compatibility and scalability. α-Lactalbumin and β-lactoglobulin are the most tractable targets given minimal PTM dependency; caseins and lactoferrin require intracellular phosphorylation and glycosylation unavailable in microbial hosts. AI accelerates process optimization but cannot yet co-optimize yield, folding fidelity, and PTM accuracy, a key frontier for next-generation engineering. Scale-up robustness, glycoengineering consistency, and regulatory definition remain underexplored.

# Metabolic Upregulation (Paper 1) — Code & Data

Computational code and data accompanying the manuscript
**"Genome-Scale Metabolic Models Identify Metabolic Bottlenecks in Production of
Recombinant Proteins in *Komagataella phaffii*"** (Acharya et al.).

This repository reproduces the modeling and figure pipeline of the paper: adapting
the *K. phaffii* GEM iMT1026v3 to produce four recombinant proteins (VHH, RBD, HSA,
IgG1), identifying overexpression/knockout targets by FSEOF, nominating transcription-
factor targets, and computing per-gene nutrient cost.

> Extracted from the larger `Kpha_GEM_Expansion` research repository; only the files
> required for this paper are included.

## Requirements

| Tool | Version | Used for |
|------|---------|----------|
| MATLAB | R2024a | model build, FBA/FSEOF, cost pipeline |
| Gurobi | 9.5+ | LP/MILP solver for MATLAB |
| COBRA Toolbox | v3.0 | constraint-based modeling |
| RAVEN Toolbox | 2.0 | model I/O (`importModel`) and utilities |
| R | 4.5.0 | figure generation and statistics |

R packages: `tidyverse`, `readxl`, `janitor`, `ggplot2`, `fgsea`/`gmtPathways`, `patchwork`.

## Setup

1. Install MATLAB, Gurobi, COBRA v3.0, and RAVEN 2.0.
2. Open **`setup_solver.m`** and edit it to point to your Gurobi install (and, if not
   already on your MATLAB path, COBRA and RAVEN). Each MATLAB script calls this
   automatically and adds `matlab/functions/` to the path — you do not need to set
   paths per script.
3. Run any script from `matlab/scripts/**` directly (the scripts locate the repo root
   themselves via `mfilename`, so the working directory does not matter).

## Layout

```
Paper1_Code_and_Data/
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── CITATION.cff
├── .gitignore
├── setup_solver.m                  ← edit this once (Gurobi/COBRA/RAVEN paths)
├── matlab/
│   ├── scripts/
│   │   ├── 01_HSA_target_identification/       HSA GEM build + validation + FSEOF (Fig 1, Fig 2a,b)
│   │   ├── 02_common_target_identification/    4-protein GEMs + FSEOF + common targets (Fig 1, Fig 2c,d)
│   │   ├── 03_transcription_factor_targets/    TF–gene network (Fig 3)
│   │   └── 04_nutrient_cost/                   per-gene nutrient cost pipeline (Fig 4, SI §5)
│   └── functions/modelBuilding/    17 custom reaction builders required by the scripts
│                                    (translation, N-/O-glyc, disulfide, COPII transport, PTMs)
├── models/                         base GEM iMT1026v3 (see Provenance)
├── data/                           model-modification + gene-property inputs
├── R/                              figure & statistics notebooks
│   ├── Figs.Rmd                    master figure notebook → publication SVGs
│   ├── geneTargetAnalysis.Rmd      gene-target / GO analysis (Fig 2 support)
│   ├── 03_TF_Graphs.Rmd            TF graphs (Fig 3 support)
│   └── figure_data/                inputs the R notebooks read
└── verification/                   transfer-integrity checks (see below)
```

## Run order and figure map

MATLAB (produces the modeling outputs and intermediate CSVs):

| Script | Produces | Manuscript |
|--------|----------|-----------|
| `matlab/scripts/01_HSA_target_identification/HSA_model_Generation_Verification.m` | HSA GEM, carbon-source validation, FSEOF slopes, gene-target table | Fig 1 (HSA), Fig 2a,b |
| `matlab/scripts/02_common_target_identification/common_target_identification_validation.m` | four-protein GEMs, cross-protein FSEOF (`FSEOF_results_*.csv`), `commonTargets.csv` | Fig 1, Fig 2c,d |
| `matlab/scripts/03_transcription_factor_targets/tf_target_analysis.m` | TF→gene directed-graph figures | Fig 3 |
| `matlab/scripts/04_nutrient_cost/metCostDetermination.m` | per-gene nutrient/protein cost (`synthCost_*.csv`) | Fig 4, SI §5 |
| `matlab/scripts/04_nutrient_cost/metCostKOBenchmark.m` | cost-based KO benchmark | Fig 4 support |

R (renders the final publication figures from the MATLAB/experimental outputs):

| Notebook | Produces |
|----------|----------|
| `R/Figs.Rmd` | Fig 1c/d, Fig 2abc/d, Fig 3b/c/d, Fig 4/4b, Fig 5, and SI cost figures (SVG/PDF, written into `R/`) |
| `R/geneTargetAnalysis.Rmd` | gene-target enrichment/analysis supporting Fig 2 |
| `R/03_TF_Graphs.Rmd` | transcription-factor graphs supporting Fig 3 |

FSEOF itself is implemented inline in scripts 01 and 02 (local function `FSEOF_custom`),
following Choi et al. 2010.

## Data & model provenance

- `models/MODEL1612130000.xml`, `models/mbt212871sup0003AppendixS3.xml` — the base
  *K. phaffii* GEM **iMT1026v3** (Tomàs-Gamisans et al.), two source encodings from
  the EBI BioModels entry <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biomodels/MODEL1612130000>. Script 01
  loads the first, script 02 the second; they are the same model. Redistribution here
  is under the source's terms — verify licensing before publishing.
- `models/iMT1026v3.mat` — the same model as a MATLAB struct (used by the cost pipeline).
- `data/baselineModifications.xlsx` — metabolites and reactions added to the base model
  (two sheets: *New Metabolites*, *New Reactions*).
- `data/ppPSIMv3_RP.csv` — per-gene protein-property table (sequence, localization,
  PTM counts, signal-peptide/GPI/TM flags) consolidated per SI §5.1.
- `data/geneConversion.csv` — GQ67 ↔ PAS locus-tag map with functional annotation.
- `data/essentiality.csv` — gene-essentiality reference used to annotate targets.

## Verification

After copying/cloning, confirm the transfer is complete (see `verification/`):

- **`verification/verify_files.py`** — cross-platform file/reference check. Run:
  `python verification/verify_files.py` from the repo root. Confirms every expected
  script, function, model, data, and R input is present, and that each path referenced
  by the scripts resolves inside the repo.
- **`verification/verify_matlab_dependencies.m`** — authoritative dependency check.
  Run in MATLAB from the repo root. Uses `matlab.codetools.requiredFilesAndProducts`
  on each entry script to compute the true required-file set, flags anything required
  but missing, reports the external toolboxes each script needs (COBRA/RAVEN/Gurobi),
  and lists any bundled function not actually required (safe-to-prune candidates).

## Citation

If you use this code or data, please cite:

> Acharya, R.; Cha, E.; Atufa, A.; Wang, E.; Narayanan, H.; Sunday, B. C.; Love, J. C. *Genome-Scale Metabolic Models Identify Metabolic Bottlenecks in Production of Recombinant Proteins in Komagataella phaffii.* (2026).

   already on your MATLAB path, COBRA and RAVEN). Each MATLAB script calls this
   automatically and adds `matlab/functions/` to the path — you do not need to set
   paths per script.
3. Run any script from `matlab/scripts/**` directly (the scripts locate the repo root
   themselves via `mfilename`, so the working directory does not matter).

## Layout

```
Paper1_Code_and_Data/
├── README.md
├── LICENSE
├── CITATION.cff
├── .gitignore
├── setup_solver.m                  ← edit this once (Gurobi/COBRA/RAVEN paths)
├── matlab/
│   ├── scripts/
│   │   ├── 01_HSA_target_identification/       HSA GEM build + validation + FSEOF (Fig 1, Fig 2a,b)
│   │   ├── 02_common_target_identification/    4-protein GEMs + FSEOF + common targets (Fig 1, Fig 2c,d)
│   │   ├── 03_transcription_factor_targets/    TF–gene network (Fig 3)
│   │   └── 04_nutrient_cost/                   per-gene nutrient cost pipeline (Fig 4, SI §5)
│   └── functions/modelBuilding/    17 custom reaction builders required by the scripts
│                                    (translation, N-/O-glyc, disulfide, COPII transport, PTMs)
├── models/                         base GEM iMT1026v3 (see Provenance)
├── data/                           model-modification + gene-property inputs
├── R/                              figure & statistics notebooks
│   ├── Figs.Rmd                    master figure notebook → publication SVGs
│   ├── geneTargetAnalysis.Rmd      gene-target / GO analysis (Fig 2 support)
│   ├── 03_TF_Graphs.Rmd            TF graphs (Fig 3 support)
│   └── figure_data/                inputs the R notebooks read
└── verification/                   transfer-integrity checks (see below)
```

## Run order and figure map

MATLAB (produces the modeling outputs and intermediate CSVs):

| Script | Produces | Manuscript |
|--------|----------|-----------|
| `matlab/scripts/01_HSA_target_identification/HSA_model_Generation_Verification.m` | HSA GEM, carbon-source validation, FSEOF slopes, gene-target table | Fig 1 (HSA), Fig 2a,b |
| `matlab/scripts/02_common_target_identification/common_target_identification_validation.m` | four-protein GEMs, cross-protein FSEOF (`FSEOF_results_*.csv`), `commonTargets.csv` | Fig 1, Fig 2c,d |
| `matlab/scripts/03_transcription_factor_targets/tf_target_analysis.m` | TF→gene directed-graph figures | Fig 3 |
| `matlab/scripts/04_nutrient_cost/metCostDetermination.m` | per-gene nutrient/protein cost (`synthCost_*.csv`) | Fig 4, SI §5 |
| `matlab/scripts/04_nutrient_cost/metCostKOBenchmark.m` | cost-based KO benchmark | Fig 4 support |

R (renders the final publication figures from the MATLAB/experimental outputs):

| Notebook | Produces |
|----------|----------|
| `R/Figs.Rmd` | Fig 1c/d, Fig 2abc/d, Fig 3b/c/d, Fig 4/4b, Fig 5, and SI cost figures (SVG/PDF, written into `R/`) |
| `R/geneTargetAnalysis.Rmd` | gene-target enrichment/analysis supporting Fig 2 |
| `R/03_TF_Graphs.Rmd` | transcription-factor graphs supporting Fig 3 |

FSEOF itself is implemented inline in scripts 01 and 02 (local function `FSEOF_custom`),
following Choi et al. 2010.

## Data & model provenance

- `models/MODEL1612130000.xml`, `models/mbt212871sup0003AppendixS3.xml` — the base
  *K. phaffii* GEM **iMT1026v3** (Tomàs-Gamisans et al.), two source encodings from
  the EBI BioModels entry <https://www.ebi.ac.uk/biomodels/MODEL1612130000>. Script 01
  loads the first, script 02 the second; they are the same model. Redistribution here
  is under the source's terms — verify licensing before publishing.
- `models/iMT1026v3.mat` — the same model as a MATLAB struct (used by the cost pipeline).
- `data/baselineModifications.xlsx` — metabolites and reactions added to the base model
  (two sheets: *New Metabolites*, *New Reactions*).
- `data/ppPSIMv3_RP.csv` — per-gene protein-property table (sequence, localization,
  PTM counts, signal-peptide/GPI/TM flags) consolidated per SI §5.1.
- `data/geneConversion.csv` — GQ67 ↔ PAS locus-tag map with functional annotation.
- `data/essentiality.csv` — gene-essentiality reference used to annotate targets.

## Verification

After copying/cloning, confirm the transfer is complete (see `verification/`):

- **`verification/verify_files.py`** — cross-platform file/reference check. Run:
  `python verification/verify_files.py` from the repo root. Confirms every expected
  script, function, model, data, and R input is present, and that each path referenced
  by the scripts resolves inside the repo.
- **`verification/verify_matlab_dependencies.m`** — authoritative dependency check.
  Run in MATLAB from the repo root. Uses `matlab.codetools.requiredFilesAndProducts`
  on each entry script to compute the true required-file set, flags anything required
  but missing, reports the external toolboxes each script needs (COBRA/RAVEN/Gurobi),
  and lists any bundled function not actually required (safe-to-prune candidates).

TITLE: Harnessing Fungal Secretion Systems for Precision Fermentation of Food Proteins.
J: ACS synthetic biology 2025 DOI: 10.1021/acssynbio.5c00521 PMCID: None
ABS: Precision fermentation is emerging as an innovative platform for manufacturing high-value food proteins, relocating food production from agricultural fields to controlled bioreactors. Importantly, these proteins must preserve the precise amino acid composition and structural properties that underpin the functionality, texture, and nutritional value of their animal-derived counterparts. However, bulk food proteins are high-volume, low-value products and therefore need to be produced at scale as cheaply as possible. Currently, intracellular protein expression requires costly cell-lysis and downstream purification steps, which comprise product purity and generally result in the product not being cost-competitive with conventional agriculture. Thus, the commercial viability of lab-grown food proteins including animal-free dairy, egg, and collagen hinges on the capacity of microbial hosts, primarily yeasts and filamentous fungi, to export correctly folded proteins into the culture medium at gram-per-liter titers, in a process known as protein secretion. Yeast and fungi are ideal host organisms due to their potential for high-yield secretion and ability to reproduce many eukaryotic post-translational modifications. Accordingly, the protein secretory pathway now sits at the crucial intersection of synthetic biology, protein engineering, and bioprocess optimization. This perspective will address modifications to the secretory pathway that can improve protein secretion efficiency. Deliberate, data-driven engineering of secretion efficiency will determine whether precision-fermented proteins advance from pilot production to routine industrial manufacture. This perspective will also address the issues of cost efficiency and scalability, exploring how protein secretion can overcome these challenges to make lab-grown food a sustainable, ethical, and viable alternative to conventional food sources.

TITLE: Methylotrophic yeast engineering for secreted protein production via precision fermentation: food ingredient proteins and synthetic biology strategies.
J: Metabolic engineering 2027 DOI: 10.1016/j.ymben.2026.102532 PMCID: None
ABS: Methylotrophic yeasts are outstanding platforms for the production of recombinant proteins through precision fermentation. Growing demand for protein-based food ingredients requires economically viable secretion efficiency and space-time yields, as well as correct post-translational modifications to ensure proper food functionality. Here, we review recent advances and future potential in engineering methylotrophic yeasts for food protein production, with particular focus on Komagataella phaffii. We first summarise the production of three categories of protein food ingredients: recombinant dairy proteins, proteins for plant-based and cultivated meat applications, and sweet-tasting proteins. Addressing the dual goals of improving both yield and quality, we then review synthetic biology and metabolic engineering strategies in methylotrophic yeasts, with emphasis on genome engineering and gene expression tools, protein secretory pathway engineering, and glycoengineering. Further advances in synthetic biology, integrated with industrial process development, will be critical to unlocking future precision fermentation systems based on methylotrophic yeasts.

TITLE: Genome-scale metabolic model of methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris and its use for in silico analysis of heterologous protein production.
J: Biotechnology journal 2010 DOI: 10.1002/biot.201000078 PMCID: None
ABS: The methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris has gained much attention during the last decade as a platform for producing heterologous recombinant proteins of pharmaceutical importance, due to its ability to reproduce post-translational modification similar to higher eukaryotes. With the recent release of the full genome sequence for P. pastoris, in-depth study of its functions has become feasible. Here we present the first reconstruction of the genome-scale metabolic model of the eukaryote P. pastoris type strain DSMZ 70382, PpaMBEL1254, consisting of 1254 metabolic reactions and 1147 metabolites compartmentalized into eight different regions to represent organelles. Additionally, equations describing the production of two heterologous proteins, human serum albumin and human superoxide dismutase, were incorporated. The protein-producing model versions of PpaMBEL1254 were then analyzed to examine the impact on oxygen limitation on protein production.

TITLE: Model based engineering of Pichia pastoris central metabolism enhances recombinant protein production.
J: Metabolic engineering 2014 DOI: 10.1016/j.ymben.2014.05.011 PMCID: PMC4094982
ABS: The production of recombinant proteins is frequently enhanced at the levels of transcription, codon usage, protein folding and secretion. Overproduction of heterologous proteins, however, also directly affects the primary metabolism of the producing cells. By incorporation of the production of a heterologous protein into a genome scale metabolic model of the yeast Pichia pastoris, the effects of overproduction were simulated and gene targets for deletion or overexpression for enhanced productivity were predicted. Overexpression targets were localized in the pentose phosphate pathway and the TCA cycle, while knockout targets were found in several branch points of glycolysis. Five out of 9 tested targets led to an enhanced production of cytosolic human superoxide dismutase (hSOD). Expression of bacterial β-glucuronidase could be enhanced as well by most of the same genetic modifications. Beneficial mutations were mainly related to reduction of the NADP/H pool and the deletion of fermentative pathways. Overexpression of the hSOD gene itself had a strong impact on intracellular fluxes, most of which changed in the same direction as predicted by the model. In vivo fluxes changed in the same direction as predicted to improve hSOD production. Genome scale metabolic modeling is shown to predict overexpression and deletion mutants which enhance recombinant protein production with high accuracy.

TITLE: Metabolic costs of amino acid and protein production in Escherichia coli.
J: Biotechnology journal 2013 DOI: 10.1002/biot.201200267 PMCID: None
ABS: Escherichia coli is the most popular microorganism for the production of recombinant proteins and is gaining increasing importance for the production of low-molecular weight compounds such as amino acids. content.content: Exit code 1 TITLE: Fine-tuning the P. pastoris iMT1026 genome-scale metabolic model for improved prediction of growth on methanol or glycerol as sole carbon sources. J: Microbial biotechnology 2018 DOI: 10.1111/1751-7915.12871 PMCID: PMC5743807 ABS: The methylotrophic yeast Pichia pastoris (Komagataella spp.) is widely used as cell factory for recombinant protein production. In the past recent years, important breakthroughs in the systems-level quantitative analysis of its physiology have been achieved. This wealth of information has allowed the development of genome-scale metabolic models, which make new approaches possible for host cell and bioprocess engineering. Nevertheless, the predictive accuracy of the previous consensus model required to be upgraded and validated with new experimental data sets for P. pastoris growing on glycerol or methanol as sole carbon sources, two of the most relevant substrates for this cell factory. In this study, we have characterized P. pastoris growing in chemostat cultures using glycerol or methanol as sole carbon sources over a wide range of growth rates, thereby providing physiological data on the effect of growth rate and culture conditions on biomass macromolecular and elemental composition. In addition, these data sets were used to improve the performance of the P. pastoris consensus genomic-scale metabolic model iMT1026. Thereupon, new experimentally determined bounds, including the representation of biomass composition for these growth conditions, have been incorporated. As a result, here, we present version 3 (v3.0) of the consensus P. pastoris genome-scale metabolic model as an update of the iMT1026 model. The v3.0 model was validated for growth on glycerol and methanol as sole carbon sources, demonstrating improved prediction capabilities over an extended substrate range including two TITLE: Genome-scale metabolic model of Pichia pastoris with native and humanized glycosylation of recombinant proteins.
J: Biotechnology and bioengineering 2016 DOI: 10.1002/bit.25863 PMCID: None
ABS: Pichia pastoris is used for commercial production of human therapeutic proteins, and genome-scale models of P. pastoris metabolism have been generated in the past to study the metabolism and associated protein production by this yeast. A major challenge with clinical usage of recombinant proteins produced by P. pastoris is the difference in N-glycosylation of proteins produced by humans and this yeast. However, through metabolic engineering, a P. pastoris strain capable of producing humanized N-glycosylated proteins was constructed. The current genome-scale models of P. pastoris do not address native nor humanized N-glycosylation, and we therefore developed ihGlycopastoris, an extension to the iLC915 model with both native and humanized N-glycosylation for recombinant protein production, but also an estimation of N-glycosylation of P. pastoris native proteins. This new model gives a better prediction of protein yield, demonstrates the effect of the different types of N-glycosylation of protein yield, and can be used to predict potential targets for strain improvement. The model represents a step towards a more complete description of protein production in P. pastoris, which is required for using these models to understand and optimize protein production processes.

# Prior-art audit: "stoichiometry-grounded, sequence-informed producibility index for recombinant food proteins in *K. phaffii* and *T. reesei*"

Adversarial audit. Date: 2026-11-18. Screened ~220 records (Europe PMC REST, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar, bioRxiv API, GitHub search, web search). Companion machine-readable list: `data/literature/papers_priorart.tsv`.

**Verdict in one line: the method is not novel; the method applied to *this* target panel, validated against *measured* literature titers, with an explicit gap decomposition against the stoichiometric ceiling, is novel but narrow. Steps (1) and (2) as written are already published — twice in yeast, once in exactly *K. phaffii*, and once under exactly the word "producibility" in exactly *T. reesei*.**

---

## 1. Table

Codes: **SCOOPS** = a published work already does this part as described; **PARTIAL** = does it in another host/product class or with a weaker readout; **ADJACENT** = relevant context, does not do it.

| Work | What it does | Scoops / partial / adjacent | What it leaves open |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Feizi et al. 2013, PLoS ONE 8:e63284** (`10.1371/journal.pone.0063284`) | Yeast secretory-machinery GEM built on a Protein Specific Information Matrix of **seven sequence features: signal peptide, N-glyc site count, O-glyc site count, disulfide count, GPI, TM, localisation**; computes **per-protein** ATP, GTP, FADH2, GDP-mannose, UDP-GlcNAc and dolichol demand for the whole proteome | **SCOOPS** the per-protein cost-from-sequence-features idea outright | Native *S. cerevisiae* proteome, not recombinant products; costs in molecules·cell⁻¹·h⁻¹, **no yield per gram substrate**; no titer validation; no food proteins; no composite index |
| **Gutierrez et al. 2020, Nat Commun 11:68** (`10.1038/s41467-019-13867-y`) | Human/mouse/CHO secretory-pathway reconstructions; "enable the computation of energetic costs and machinery demands of **each** secreted protein"; **predicts metabolic costs and maximum productivities of biotherapeutic proteins** and **identifies which protein features most significantly impact secretion** | **SCOOPS** the conceptual package (cost + maximum productivity + feature attribution) | Mammalian hosts, glucose/glutamine not glycerol/methanol; biotherapeutics; productivity is model-predicted, not regressed on published titers |
| **Li, Chen, Nielsen et al. 2022, Nat Commun 13:2969 — pcSecYeast** (`10.1038/s41467-022-30689-7`) | Proteome-constrained secretory GEM; protein-specific secretion reactions assembled **from each protein's amino-acid sequence and PTM profile**; eight recombinant proteins incl. **haemoglobin**; simulates max production rate vs growth; **SHAP feature-importance over N-glyc sites, O-glyc sites, disulfide count, TM and amino-acid composition** (5-fold CV); per-protein bottleneck calls ("for all other recombinant proteins, the secretory pathway is more limiting"; haemoglobin uniquely metabolism-limited) | **SCOOPS** steps (1)+(2) and the "which bottleneck binds for each protein" deliverable | *S. cerevisiae*; pharma panel; target variable is **simulated** production rate, not measured titer; no disorder / phosphorylation / codon / aggregation features; no g-per-g-substrate ceiling; no index artifact |
| **Acharya et al. 2026, manuscript + code (`github.com/RaghavAcharya/kphaffii-metabolic-bottlenecks`, last push 2026-10-29). NO DOI FOUND — not in Europe PMC or Crossref; cannot verify a citation** | **iMT1026v3 in exactly *K. phaffii***, adapted to four recombinant proteins (VHH, RBD, HSA, IgG1) with 17 custom builders (translation, N-/O-glycosylation, disulfide, COPII, PTMs), a **PSIM-style per-gene property table (sequence, localisation, PTM counts, signal-peptide/GPI/TM flags)**, FSEOF targets, and a **per-gene/per-protein nutrient-cost pipeline**, plus carbon-source validation | **SCOOPS** step (1) in the exact host; **PARTIAL** on step (2) | Four pharma proteins; no food proteins; no titer regression; no disorder/phosphorylation/aggregation/codon features; no *T. reesei*; **and it is unpublished, so the race is live** |
| **Dykstra, Rousu & Arvas 2017, bioRxiv `10.1101/138560`** | "Predicting Protein **Producibility** in Filamentous Fungi": supervised and semi-supervised SVMs predicting recombinant-protein producibility in **exactly *T. reesei*** (and *A. niger*) from **amino-acid composition + Pfam/domain features**, with cross-species transfer tests | **SCOOPS** the term, the host and the sequence-ML framing | Binary producible/not classification, not titer regression; no stoichiometric cost layer; no PTM/disorder/codon panel; no food proteins; **preprint only — bioRxiv reports no journal version**, so it is scoop-by-priority not scoop-by-citation-weight |
| **Arvas et al. 2016, Biotechnol Biofuels 9:170** (`10.1186/s13068-016-0547-5`) | Genome-wide protein-production-load analysis in *T. reesei*; first genome-wide stoichiometric model under protein-production conditions; **model predicts protein production rate**; nominates sulphur assimilation as the binding limit | **SCOOPS** the *T. reesei* stoichiometric-cost half | Native cellulases, not heterologous food proteins; no per-protein sequence panel; no cross-protein index |
| **Tortajada, Llaneras, Ramón & Picó 2012, J Process Control 22:1139** (`10.1016/j.jprocont.2012.03.009`) | Constraint-based *P. pastoris* model + possibilistic MFA predicts **ATP flux**, then **linearly regresses protein productivity on ATP flux** with cross-validation | **PARTIAL** — the "regress productivity on stoichiometric ATP burden" move is published | Single strain/product, online-measurement soft-sensor; no sequence features; no cross-protein comparison. (Abstract read via Semantic Scholar; publisher paywalled.) |
| **Chung et al. 2010, Biotechnol J 5:S107/PpaMBEL1254** (`10.1002/biot.201000078`) | Pichia GEM with explicit **production equations for two recombinant proteins (HSA, hSOD)**, used for in-silico analysis of heterologous protein production under O₂ limitation | **SCOOPS** "add a per-protein demand reaction built from composition" in Pichia, as of 2010 | Two pharma proteins; no feature panel; no yield ceiling table |
| **Nocon et al. 2014, Metab Eng 24:129** (`10.1016/j.ymben.2014.05.011`) | Heterologous protein synthesis embedded in a Pichia GEM; KO/OE predictions, experimentally validated | **PARTIAL** | Engineering targets, not a producibility score |
| **Irani, Kerkhoven, Shojaosadati & Nielsen 2016, Biotechnol Bioeng 113:961** (`10.1002/bit.25863`) | ihGlycopastoris: native + humanised N-glycosylation on iLC915; "**gives a better prediction of protein yield**", shows glycosylation-type effect on yield | **PARTIAL→SCOOPS** on the glycan-cost component in Pichia | Pharma/clinical framing; whether a g-per-g-substrate ceiling is reported **could not be verified — paywalled, full text not readable in this audit**; no food proteins; no titer regression |
| **Tomàs-Gamisans et al. 2018, Microb Biotechnol 11:224** (`10.1111/1751-7915.12871`) | iMT1026 **v3**, validated specifically for growth on **glycerol or methanol as sole carbon sources**, with condition-specific biomass composition | **ADJACENT** but decisive: the substrate-specific stoichiometry needed for "g protein per g glycerol/methanol" is already built and validated | Does not compute protein-specific yield ceilings; leaves the per-protein number to be computed (a one-line FBA, not a contribution) |
| **Pentjuss et al. 2023, Sci Rep 13:15816** (`10.1038/s41598-023-42865-w`) | iMT1026, *P. pastoris* X-33 legH strain, glycerol vs methanol cultivations, growth-coupled reaction ranking (own algorithm citing Choi et al. 2010, **not FSEOF**) | **ADJACENT** | **Verified from full text: reports NO maximum theoretical haem or legH yield and NO titer.** The three occurrences of "theoretical maximum" all refer to **biomass growth rate** on methanol, not product yield. Confirms the coordinator's read. (Note: corrected in Sci Rep 2025;15:33718.) The legH yield ceiling is genuinely unoccupied ground |
| **Kaleta et al. 2013, Biotechnol J 8:1105** (`10.1002/biot.201200267`) | ATP cost of each amino acid **and of recombinant proteins** from glucose, **glycerol** and acetate, by three constraint-based methods; identifies Met/Leu as costliest | **SCOOPS** step (1)'s method, in *E. coli*, including a glycerol substrate | Not yeast/fungi; no methanol; no sequence-feature panel; no specific protein panel |
| **Akashi & Gojobori 2002** (`10.1073/pnas.062526999`); **Wagner 2005** (`10.1093/molbev/msi126`); **Lynch & Marinov 2015** (`10.1073/pnas.1514974112`); **Barton et al. 2010** (`10.1371/journal.pone.0011935`); **Raiford et al. 2008** (`10.1007/s00239-008-9162-9`) | Amino-acid and per-gene biosynthetic/bioenergetic cost from composition; cost-driven selection on composition | **SCOOPS** "compute a protein's cost from its amino-acid composition" as a concept — this is 24-year-old settled method | Evolutionary questions, not bioprocess prediction; no host-specific GEM yield ceilings; no secretion |

Searched and found **nothing** for: a published producibility/tractability index for precision-fermentation food proteins; any regression of published K. phaffii or T. reesei titers on sequence features; any FBA cost comparison across casein / β-Lg / α-La / ovalbumin / leghemoglobin / lactoferrin; any *K. phaffii* or *T. reesei* proteome-constrained **secretory** GEM equivalent to pcSecYeast. These four are the only empty cells I could find.

---

## 2. Verdict: what is novel, what is not

### Not novel — cut or demote to Methods

1. **"Compute each protein's exact metabolic cost from its amino-acid composition."** Settled since Akashi & Gojobori 2002; done in a GEM with glycerol by Kaleta 2013; done per-protein from the same seven sequence features by Feizi 2013; done in *K. phaffii* with iMT1026v3 by Acharya et al. 2026. Claiming this as a contribution will not survive review. It is a **Methods subsection**.
2. **"ATP/NADPH burden per protein."** Same. Feizi 2013 and Gutierrez 2020 both report per-protein cofactor budgets.
3. **"A sequence-feature panel."** Every feature is an existing public tool, and the PTM/disorder/disulfide subset is exactly Feizi's PSIM plus SECRiFY's disorder finding. Assembly is not invention.
4. **"Says which bottleneck binds for each protein."** pcSecYeast 2022 already does per-protein bottleneck attribution (secretory vs metabolic) across eight proteins. Acharya 2026 does bottleneck identification in *K. phaffii*. Do not frame this as the novelty.
5. **"A producibility index for *T. reesei* from sequence."** Dykstra, Rousu & Arvas 2017 published this under that exact word for that exact host. You must cite it and state your delta. Failing to cite it reads as ignorance of the field.
6. **The expected ranking itself** (α-La/β-Lg easy → ovalbumin → LegH → casein hardest). Already in print, qualitatively, in `10.1111/1541-4337.70618` and restated across the 2024–2026 reviews. If your index reproduces it, you have validated a known ordering; if it contradicts it, you must explain why.
7. **A new per-kg techno-economic model.** Humbird 2021 and the GFI/industry models exist and already use stoichiometric yields. Parameterise, do not re-derive.

### Genuinely novel — the defensible core

1. **Target panel.** No published stoichiometric-cost or secretory-cost work covers food proteins. Everything cited above runs on α-amylase, insulin, HSA, hGCSF, transferrin, haemoglobin, VHH, RBD, IgG1, or native cellulases. Casein, β-lactoglobulin, α-lactalbumin, ovalbumin, leghemoglobin and lactoferrin are an empty cell. This is real but thin on its own — it is "same method, new substrate list", the weakest kind of novelty.
2. **Titer-validated regression.** This is the strongest piece. pcSecYeast and Gutierrez regress/attribute features against **model-simulated** productivity. Lin 2014 regresses against measured titers but only for CHO mAb CDR3s. Tortajada 2012 regresses productivity on ATP flux but for one strain as a soft-sensor. **Nobody has fit a cross-protein, cross-host model to the published experimental titer record for K. phaffii / T. reesei.** That requires the curated titer database you are building (`docs/TITER_DB_SPEC.md`) — the database is itself a defensible artifact and arguably more citable than the index.
3. **"Distance from the stoichiometric ceiling" gap decomposition.** Computing the maximum theoretical g protein per g glycerol/methanol per protein and then expressing each measured titer as a fraction of that ceiling, with the residual attributed to specific sequence features, is a framing I could not find anywhere. Pentjuss 2023 — the one paper closest to doing it for legH in iMT1026 — **verifiably does not report any product yield ceiling**. Gutierrez 2020 computes "maximum productivities" but does not decompose measured-vs-ceiling gaps. This is the only part of the claim with a clean mechanism-level story.
4. **Cross-host comparability** (*K. phaffii* vs *T. reesei* on a common cost basis). Minor, but no one has put the two side by side on a shared stoichiometric metric.

### The sharpest honest framing

> *Published per-protein cost and secretory-burden models (Feizi 2013; Gutierrez 2020; pcSecYeast 2022) predict production capability for pharmaceutical proteins and validate against simulations or single-product experiments. We ask instead how far the published food-protein titer record sits from the stoichiometric ceiling of its host. We compute, for each of N food proteins, the maximum theoretical g protein per g glycerol or methanol in iMT1026v3 / the T. reesei GEM; we assemble a curated titer database of M measurements; and we show that the realised fraction of the ceiling spans X orders of magnitude and is explained not by metabolic cost — which varies less than Yx across the panel — but by [disorder / glycosylation load / disulfide count]. The contribution is the gap decomposition and the titer database, not the cost calculation.*

Two load-bearing consequences of this framing:

- **The index must be allowed to fail.** The most likely and most publishable result is that **metabolic cost is NOT the binding constraint** for food proteins — amino-acid cost varies little across these sequences, while titers vary 100-fold. Pre-register that as a possible finding. "Cost is not the bottleneck, and here is the stoichiometry that proves it" is a stronger, harder-to-scoop result than a scoring tool.
- **Call it something other than "producibility index".** The word is taken (Dykstra 2017), and "index" invites the fatal "you fit a composite score to ~15 points" objection. Prefer *ceiling-gap analysis*, *stoichiometric headroom*, or *cost-versus-realised-titer decomposition*.

---

## 3. The three strongest objections, and whether they are answerable

### Objection 1 (fatal if unaddressed): "Feizi 2013, Gutierrez 2020 and pcSecYeast 2022 already compute per-protein cost from exactly your feature set. Acharya et al. 2026 already did it in *K. phaffii* with iMT1026v3. What is left?"

**Answerable — but only by conceding steps (1) and (2).** The honest answer: nothing in the cost calculation is new, and the write-up must say so in the first paragraph of the Methods, with all four citations. What survives is the **measured-titer target variable** and the **ceiling-gap decomposition** on a food-protein panel. Any draft that presents the cost pipeline as a contribution will be rejected by anyone who has read the Nielsen-lab line of work.

**Risk flag:** Acharya et al. is **unpublished**, is from a well-resourced lab (Love, MIT), its code went public on 2026-10-29, and the same group published `10.1186/s12934-026-03009-7` in 2026 on K. phaffii secretion-gene deletions. If they add food proteins or a titer regression in a Paper 2, the remaining novelty narrows further. Treat this as a race and watch that repo.

### Objection 2 (hardest to answer): "You are fitting a model to a handful of heterogeneous literature titers. That is not a predictive model, it is overfitting to a confounded dataset."

**Only partly answerable.** The published titer record for these proteins is small (order 10–100 measurements), and the dominant variance is almost certainly **not** protein identity but strain, promoter, copy number, signal peptide, cultivation mode, carbon feed and quantification method — the exact covariates your own `TITER_DB_SPEC.md` is right to record. With ~6 target proteins, a multi-feature regression has more parameters than informative points.

Honest mitigations, in order of strength:
1. **Do not fit a multi-feature predictive model at all.** Report the ceiling-gap per protein as a descriptive quantity, with a mixed-effects model where process covariates are random effects and protein identity is the fixed effect of interest. State the confidence intervals and let them be wide.
2. Expand the training set beyond food proteins to all *K. phaffii* / *T. reesei* secreted recombinant proteins with published titers (hundreds of measurements), then treat the food proteins as held-out predictions. This is the single highest-value design change available, and it is also the design that makes the Dykstra 2017 comparison explicit.
3. Report leave-one-protein-out performance and a permutation null. If the model does not beat "predict the panel mean", say so.

An examiner can and will press this. There is no framing that makes a 6-protein regression defensible; only a larger training set or an abandonment of the regression does.

### Objection 3: "Your index's output is the ranking already published qualitatively in the 2026 milk-protein review — you have quantified received wisdom."

**Answerable, and this one is winnable.** Three lines of reply: (a) the review's ranking is argued from PTM dependency alone, while the stoichiometric result may **disagree** with it — caseins are cheap, disordered, short and cysteine-free, so by metabolic cost and folding load they should be *easy*, and their difficulty is PTM/functionality, not production; demonstrating that split quantitatively is a genuine result; (b) a ceiling-gap number is actionable (it says how much headroom strain engineering has) where a tractability adjective is not; (c) the review itself names co-optimising yield, folding fidelity and PTM accuracy as an open frontier, which is a citable invitation.

**Fourth objection worth pre-empting** (an examiner who knows constraint-based modelling will raise it): *"Why a bespoke index instead of an ecModel/ME-model of K. phaffii, which would give cost, proteome allocation and bottlenecks in one object?"* Answer honestly: because no proteome-constrained secretory K. phaffii model exists yet, and because the measured-titer comparison is the point. Note also `10.1002/bit.26380` — predicted targets in K. phaffii are sensitive to the assumed biomass composition — so every cost number needs a sensitivity analysis over biomass composition and growth rate, or it will be dismissed as a point estimate with hidden error bars.

---

## 4. Answer to the framing question posed by the coordinator

> Given Feizi 2013 and Irani 2015 exist, is the defensible novelty (i) the food-protein panel, (ii) the titer-validated regression, (iii) the ceiling-gap decomposition, or (iv) some combination — and what would you cut?

**(iii) + (ii), with (i) as the setting rather than the claim. Cut the index framing entirely.**

- **(iii) ceiling-gap decomposition — keep as the headline.** It is the only element I could not find published, and Pentjuss 2023 is verifiably silent on product yield ceilings, so the legH/food-protein ceiling numbers are unoccupied. It is also the element that is robust to a small dataset, because it is a stoichiometric calculation plus a descriptive comparison, not a fitted model.
- **(ii) titer-validated regression — keep, but demote to a validated descriptive analysis and only if the training set is widened beyond the food panel.** As a 6-protein predictive model it is indefensible (Objection 2). The **curated titer database** is the durable artifact here and should be released and cited in its own right.
- **(i) food-protein panel — keep as the setting, not the novelty.** "Same method, new substrate list" is the weakest available claim and invites the comparison to Acharya et al. Say plainly: these are the proteins that matter commercially and none of the existing cost models cover them.
- **Cut:** the word "producibility" (taken by Dykstra 2017 for exactly *T. reesei*); any claim to novelty in the cost calculation, the ATP/NADPH accounting, the sequence-feature panel, or per-protein bottleneck attribution; and any new per-kg techno-economic model.

**Also do these, concretely:**
- Cite Feizi 2013, Gutierrez 2020, pcSecYeast 2022, Dykstra 2017, Arvas 2016, Kaleta 2013 and Acharya 2026 (as an unpublished preprint/code reference) in the first Methods paragraph. The audit's biggest finding is not a missing gap — it is a **citation gap**.
- Verify whether Irani 2016 (`10.1002/bit.25863`) reports a g-per-g-substrate yield anywhere, including supplementary. **I could not: the paper is paywalled and no OA full text was reachable in this audit.** If it does, the ceiling claim weakens and must be rephrased as "first for food proteins on glycerol and methanol".
- Monitor `github.com/RaghavAcharya/kphaffii-metabolic-bottlenecks` and Europe PMC for the Acharya et al. publication.

---

## 5. Verification notes

- All DOIs and PMIDs in the table and in `papers_priorart.tsv` were retrieved live from Europe PMC REST, Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or the bioRxiv API during this audit. None were recalled from memory.
- **Unverified / explicitly flagged:** (a) **Acharya et al. 2026 has no DOI** — absent from Europe PMC and Crossref; the only citable artifact is the public GitHub repository. (b) The **Tortajada 2012** abstract was read via the Semantic Scholar API, not the publisher (ScienceDirect blocked). DOI confirmed via Crossref. (c) **Irani 2016** full text could not be read; only the Europe PMC abstract. (d) The **SignalP 6.0** record given is the bioRxiv preprint; the journal version was not verified. (e) Pentjuss 2023's **2025 correction** (Sci Rep 15:33718) is noted in the article record but its content was not read.
- Pentjuss 2023's absence of a yield/titer number was verified by full-text search of the Europe PMC XML (PMC10516909): zero matches for "titer"/"titre", zero for "maximum theoretical", three for "theoretical maximum" — all referring to biomass growth rate — and zero for "FSEOF".

| **secCellFie** (`10.1016/j.ymben.2023.12.006`); **"Evolutionary adaptation of the folding pathway for secretability"** (`10.15252/embj.2022111344`) | Productised secretory-pathway scoring from omics; folding-pathway determinants of secretability | **ADJACENT** | Shows per-protein secretory scoring is already a tool category |
| **Lin et al. 2014, Biotechnol Prog 31:1** (`10.1002/btpr.1839`) | Predicts **measured** CHO mAb titer from **coding-sequence features** across a product panel, with error reported in expression units | **SCOOPS** the "sequence features → measured titer regression" design, in CHO | Antibody CDR3 only; one host, one process; no stoichiometric cost; not transferable to food proteins |
| **Lauer et al. 2012, J Pharm Sci 101:102 — Developability Index** (`10.1002/jps.22758`) | A single sequence/structure-derived number screening manufacturability (aggregation propensity) | **SCOOPS** the *genre*: composite in-silico producibility indices are a 14-year-old accepted device | Antibodies, aggregation only |

It explicitly names co-optimising yield/folding/PTM as "a key frontier". That sentence is the open door |
| **"Methylotrophic yeast engineering … food ingredient proteins" Metab Eng 2027** (`10.1016/j.ymben.2026.102532`); **"Harnessing Fungal Secretion Systems for Precision Fermentation of Food Proteins" ACS Synth Biol 2025** (`10.1021/acssynbio.5c00521`) | Reviews of K. phaffii / fungal food-protein production emphasising secretion efficiency, space-time yield, PTM fidelity, and cost | **ADJACENT** | Narrative, no per-protein numbers. Both would be cited *by* the index, not against it |
